newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters resume strike talks Thursday.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters resume strike talks Thursday.

text.p: Labor Secretary Alexis Herman announced on Wednesday the Teamsters and United Parcel Service agreed to go back to the bargaining table on Thursday, and urged them to talk until they strike a deal.

Neither side has budged during a 10-day-old strike, one of the largest in the past quarter century, and Teamsters President Ron Carey was pessimistic the meeting could breathe new life into talks aimed at ending a dispute that has idled 185,000 Teamsters and cost hundreds of millions of dollars.
"While there is no reason for optimism at this point we will be there, ready to negotiate a reasonable agreement that provides the good jobs that American families need," Carey said in a statement.
UPS Chairman James Kelly said of the new talks, "We remain open and willing to examine all avenues that will help our people get back to work."
The two sides are scheduled to meet at 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) with federal mediator John Calhoun Wells, who has moderated the past two unsuccessful rounds of talks.
Herman said that "the key now is for both parties to find a new way to look at the issues and find a solution at the table," and she urged them "to stay at the table until they reach a settlement."
Talks broke off Saturday, when Kelly left the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, calling the Teamster position "unrealistic."
Kelly and the Teamsters' Carey agreed on one thing: Neither side was willing to compromise.
The parties also talked earlier, and when those talks broke down the strike began at 12:01 a.m. (0401 GMT) on Aug. 4.

Herman called both sides into her office this week and they met on Monday. But the two sides hardened their positions on Tuesday, when the AFL-CIO offered millions of dollars to help the Teamsters pay strike benefits to people on picket lines, while UPS warned it will cut 15,000 jobs because of lost business.
But even as the two sides seemed to dig in, the impact of the strike spread.

Russ Berrie and Co. Inc., an Oakland, N.J.-based maker of plush dolls and gift items, and National TechTeam Inc., which provides technical services to UPS customers, each said they cut about 100 workers.

"At this time of year, we're shipping a lot of seasonal and Christmas items. We can't find enough sources to get out the products," Russ Berrie President Curts Cooke said, adding the company's shipments were about 25 percent of normal.

National TechTeam, based in Dearborn, Mich., said it laid off about 100 employees who worked with a 175-member team that provides technical support to customers tied to UPS' computer system. Chief Executive William Coyro said the company would place the workers in temporary slots on other projects until the UPS strike ends.

If there is to be an end to the strike, it appears it will have to come from the parties. White House spokesman Mike McCurry gave no sign that U.S. President Bill Clinton would change his mind and step in.

"As a general premise, we take the view that government should not step in and resolve labor-management disputes, that they ought to be resolved by the parties through collective bargaining," McCurry said during his daily briefing.
The Independent Pilots Association of UPS pilots -- which has refused to cross Teamster picket lines to fly 500 UPS planes -- issued a warning to pilots whose airlines were carrying UPS packages.
"Effective on Friday, Aug. 15 ... all flights carrying struck UPS goods will be considered strike-breaking activity," the union said. It scheduled a news conference for Thursday.

An ABC News poll released late Tuesday showed 40 percent of Americans backed the union in its fight to win more higher-paying, full-time jobs. UPS won 30 percent support in the survey of 506 adults conducted on Monday, while 30 percent said they were neutral.
The poll also showed support for Clinton's position, indicating 64 percent of those polled opposed presidential intervention in the strike.
To intervene, Clinton would have to seek a court order under the Taft-Hartley law, last used by President Jimmy Carter in 1978.

Carter intervened when a coal miners strike dragged on for three months and won a court order that was largely ignored. Carter lost in court on March 17, 1978, when a federal judge refused to extend the order, citing the absence of "evidence of irreparable harm to the national health or safety."
